q: During a cemented hemiarthroplasty, the patient's SpO2 falls to 88% and systolic BP falls by 45% without loss of consciousness. What grade of bone cement implantation syndrome is this?
o: It does not meet BCIS criteria
why: Donaldson grading: grade 1 = SpO2 < 94% or systolic fall > 20%; grade 2 = SpO2 < 88% or systolic fall > 40% or unexpected loss of consciousness; grade 3 = cardiovascular collapse needing CPR. A fall to 88% with a 45% systolic drop is grade 2. Joint AAGBI/BOA/BGS guidance: identify high-risk patients, the surgeon washes and dries the canal and uses a retrograde cementing gun, the anaesthetist maintains vigilance and BP, and roles are briefed.

q: An 85-year-old on warfarin for AF (INR 2.8) has a hip fracture. What is the most appropriate plan for surgery?
o: Wait for the INR to fall naturally to below 1.5
Give prothrombin complex concentrate routinely to everyone
Give IV vitamin K (e.g. 5 mg) and plan surgery within 36 hours, using GA or spinal according to the INR on the day
why: Hip fracture surgery should happen within 36 hours of admission (NICE/BOAST). Warfarin should be reversed with IV vitamin K, rechecking INR in 4–6 hours; spinal anaesthesia is acceptable at INR ≤ 1.5 (some accept slightly higher with senior input). PCC is reserved for urgent reversal for bleeding or emergency surgery. Delaying surgery while waiting for spontaneous reversal increases mortality.

q: Thirty-six hours after a femoral shaft fracture, a young man becomes confused and hypoxic with a petechial rash on the axillae and conjunctivae. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Supportive care with oxygen and ventilatory support as needed
why: Fat embolism syndrome (Gurd's major criteria: respiratory insufficiency, cerebral signs, petechial rash) appears 24–72 hours after long-bone or pelvic fractures. Treatment is supportive. Early fixation of long-bone fractures reduces incidence. Steroid prophylaxis is not routinely recommended; heparin and thrombolysis have no role.

q: Which strategy most reduces blood transfusion during posterior spinal fusion for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis?
o: Tranexamic acid with cell salvage, and prone positioning with a free abdomen
why: Blood conservation in spinal fusion uses tranexamic acid (strong evidence), cell salvage, preoperative optimisation of haemoglobin, a free abdomen in the prone position to reduce venous congestion of epidural veins, normothermia and judicious controlled hypotension. Monitoring of spinal cord function (SSEPs/MEPs with TIVA) guides safety.

q: A 60-year-old with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis falls and has neck pain. He has a fixed flexed neck. Which statement is most important for his airway management?
o: Treat as an unstable cervical fracture until proven otherwise, keep his usual flexed posture, and plan awake or fibreoptic intubation
His spine is rigid so it cannot be injured
Place in a standard collar in neutral position
Neuraxial techniques are easy in AS
why: Ankylosed spines fracture with minor trauma and fractures are often unstable and missed on plain films (CT/MRI needed). Forcing the neck into a neutral collar can cause cord injury; immobilise in the patient's normal position. Airway management is often difficult (fixed flexion, limited mouth opening from TMJ involvement), so awake fibreoptic techniques are favoured. Also consider restrictive lung disease, aortic regurgitation and heart block.
